prompt: A bathtub full of water and a small cup of water are both at 40 °C. A student drops ice cubes into each until the water stops melting them. The bathtub melts far more ice than the cup. Which statement best explains this?
choices: The tub water is at a higher temperature, because a larger amount of water stays hotter.
Cold from the ice spreads out into the big tub, so more of the ice can melt there.
Each drop of tub water carries more thermal energy than each drop of cup water.
Both are at 40 °C, but the tub holds far more water, so it has much more thermal energy to give.
correct_answer: Both are at 40 °C, but the tub holds far more water, so it has much more thermal energy to give.
explanation: Temperature measures the average motion of the particles, and both waters are at 40 °C. Thermal energy also depends on how much matter there is. The tub holds far more water, so it has much more thermal energy to transfer to ice before it cools down.

distractor_rationales.choice: The tub water is at a higher temperature, because a larger amount of water stays hotter.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: a larger amount of a substance has a higher temperature; both waters read 40 °C

distractor_rationales.choice: Cold from the ice spreads out into the big tub, so more of the ice can melt there.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: cold is a substance that flows or spreads; thermal energy moves from the water into the ice

distractor_rationales.choice: Each drop of tub water carries more thermal energy than each drop of cup water.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: at the same temperature, particles in a larger sample carry more energy each; the average energy per particle is the same

real_world_check: Two samples of the same substance at the same temperature have the same average particle energy, but the larger sample holds more total thermal energy and can melt more ice (MS-PS3-4).

prompt: Sofia and Victor stand on skateboards, facing each other. Victor has twice Sofia's mass. They press their hands together and push off, and Sofia rolls away faster than Victor. Which statement correctly explains the forces during the push?
choices: Each one pushes on the other with a force of equal size.
Victor pushes harder because he has more mass to push with.
Sofia feels the larger force, which is why she rolls away faster.
The skater who starts the push puts the larger force on the other one.
correct_answer: Each one pushes on the other with a force of equal size.
explanation: The forces in an interaction come in pairs that are equal in size and opposite in direction. Sofia rolls away faster because the same size force acts on her smaller mass, which gives her a greater change in motion.

distractor_rationales.choice: Victor pushes harder because he has more mass to push with.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: the object with more mass exerts the larger force in an interaction

distractor_rationales.choice: Sofia feels the larger force, which is why she rolls away faster.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: the faster-moving object must have felt the larger force; her smaller mass explains her speed

distractor_rationales.choice: The skater who starts the push puts the larger force on the other one.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: the one who acts first pushes harder; paired forces are equal no matter who starts

real_world_check: By Newton's third law, the forces two objects exert on each other are equal in size and opposite in direction, whatever their masses (MS-PS2-1).

prompt: A space probe is launched from Earth and travels toward Mars. Its mass does not change during the trip. Which prediction about the gravitational pull between Earth and the probe is correct as the probe moves away from Earth?
choices: The pull stops completely once the probe has climbed above Earth's air.
The pull stays the same the whole way, since the probe's mass does not change.
Earth pulls on the probe at every point of the trip, but more weakly as the distance grows.
The pull grows stronger as the probe picks up more and more speed on its way to Mars.
correct_answer: Earth pulls on the probe at every point of the trip, but more weakly as the distance grows.
explanation: Gravity acts between any two masses at any distance, so Earth never stops pulling on the probe. The pull depends on the masses and on the distance between them; as the distance grows, the pull gets weaker.

distractor_rationales.choice: The pull stops completely once the probe has climbed above Earth's air.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: there is no gravity in space, or gravity needs air; gravity reaches through empty space

distractor_rationales.choice: The pull stays the same the whole way, since the probe's mass does not change.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: gravitational force depends only on mass; it also weakens with distance

distractor_rationales.choice: The pull grows stronger as the probe picks up more and more speed on its way to Mars.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: gravity depends on how fast an object moves; speed does not set the pull

real_world_check: Gravitational force between two objects depends on their masses and gets weaker, but never reaches zero, as the distance between them increases (MS-PS2-4).

prompt: A 2 kg cart rolls along a level track at 3 m/s. A student then sends the same cart along the track at 6 m/s. Which prediction about the cart's kinetic energy at 6 m/s is correct?
choices: The kinetic energy stays the same, since the cart has the same mass as before.
The kinetic energy doubles, since kinetic energy grows in step with speed.
The kinetic energy rises by the same amount it would if the mass doubled instead.
The kinetic energy becomes four times as large, because it depends on the square of the speed.
correct_answer: The kinetic energy becomes four times as large, because it depends on the square of the speed.
explanation: Kinetic energy is one half of mass times speed squared. Doubling the speed from 3 m/s to 6 m/s multiplies the speed squared by 4, so the kinetic energy goes from 9 J to 36 J, four times as much.

distractor_rationales.choice: The kinetic energy stays the same, since the cart has the same mass as before.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: kinetic energy depends only on mass; it also depends on speed

distractor_rationales.choice: The kinetic energy doubles, since kinetic energy grows in step with speed.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: kinetic energy is proportional to speed; it is proportional to speed squared

distractor_rationales.choice: The kinetic energy rises by the same amount it would if the mass doubled instead.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: mass and speed affect kinetic energy equally; doubling mass doubles it, doubling speed makes it four times as large

real_world_check: Kinetic energy equals one half of mass times speed squared, so doubling speed makes the kinetic energy four times as large while doubling mass only doubles it (MS-PS3-1).

prompt: A sealed steel tank holds helium gas. The tank is heated. Its volume cannot change, and no gas can get in or out. Which quantity of the gas increases?
explanation: Adding thermal energy to a gas makes its particles move faster, so their average speed rises along with the temperature. The particles themselves do not grow, and with no gas getting in or out, the number of particles and the mass stay the same.

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: particles expand when heated; they move faster but stay the same size
misconception: heating adds mass to a substance; thermal energy has no mass to add, and no gas entered

real_world_check: When thermal energy is added to a gas in a sealed rigid container, the average speed of its particles and its temperature increase while its mass and particle count stay the same (MS-PS1-4).
